findings.quote: These patterns have limits. *Friendly* ends in *-ly*, but it describes a person or thing, so it is an adjective.
findings.problem: The lesson teaches the misleading -ly adjective ending as a distinct limitation, but no worked example asks the student to apply it. Example 9 uses only the regular adverb quickly. The -less meaning is also taught without a worked application.

checked: All nine worked solutions use two numbered steps. The steps show how the word part or sentence job supports the answer; no computational display is needed.

L21.note: There are no display equations in this language lesson.

checked: Teaching paragraphs have one to three short sentences. The single English-element bullet list gives six compact entries; remaining explanations use paragraphs.

L23.note: There are no illustration placeholders or figure-dependent questions.

checked: Root, base, affix, stem, prefix, suffix, and infer are defined before use in the tasks. Noun, adjective, adverb, and verb are defined before the suffix teaching. Filipino terms get local definitions and examples; morphology and phonological are removed.

English suffixes are explained through meaning and word job. Filipino -um- and -in- receive sentence-level action/focus explanations, ka-...-an gives the meaning of kabataan, and laguhan is tied to effort in pinagsumikapan. Valid parsing is explained using unhappy versus uncle.

Warnings limit letter-based splitting, say older elements can be bound parts, explain that word parts are partial clues, show friendly as an -ly adjective exception, and state that Filipino affixes do not have one use in every word.
